tweets.text:
OpenAI says "GPT‑6 Cyber" identified 80+ previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox & helped develop candidate patches

This makes the economics of open-source work more interesting... as agents become capable of finding bugs + proposing fixes, we need ways to fund that work and reward contributions maintainers actually accept

That’s why I’m watching @SlopCash when it goes live on Tuesday (Nov 10)

Projects fund monthly USDC pools that reward humans + AI agents for code maintainers merge and reviews they accept, keeping maintainers in control of what gets included

As the diagram shows, Slop scores those contributions + publishes proposed rewards for 14 days of public review. Funders then approve + pay contributors directly from wallets Slop doesn’t control

My interest is whether that combination can make useful contributions worth doing repeatedly, while keeping the team accountable for how it spends the money raised

Slop’s auction on @umia_finance reached its commitment cap < 15 minutes after public bidding opened... 

Umia uses an onchain treasury, a fixed monthly team budget + decision-market approval for extra spending, with team tokens tied to long-term vesting and sustained price milestones

Worth paying attention to more launches coming down the UMIA pipeline in the coming months

Collection of distracting terms that feel ominous, but aren't once you look at the numbers / structure.
* Pvt credit a mere 5% of bank assets in size, modest leverage & funded by unlevered investors (retail/pension). 
* AI financing is mostly fwd contracts not traditional debt & the credit risk that comes with it.
* SRT gets is <1% of total bank assets and *improved* bank stability by diversifying credit risk holders. 
* Treasury debt term below LT avg.

That doesn't mean there are no risks in the financial system.  But this is weak popular financial press stuff, not serious analysis.  

If you ever want to have a real convo on it, happy to do it.

tweets.text:
Various commentary from Qualcomm, Arm, to Meta executives this week during the AI selloff: 

$LITE CEO: "You had a comment from the CEO of $IREN and I'd second that. There's a massive disconnect in what we're seeing in our demand books. 

And what the markets are showing. And yet you're seeing a massive, massive selloff." (Fri, Nov 6)

$AMD CEO CNBC: "We're at the very beginning of the adoption cycle, where people can see where AI and superintelligence will take us" 

"We are seeing demand being higher than supply" (Wed, Nov 4)

$ARM CEO regarding a debate whether AI infrastructure spending is about to peak:

"I think in some states where it gets harder, other states may pick it up to make it easier, but I do believe strongly that if the US hesitates in any way shape performance in terms of data center buildout...

"The rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity. And I think globally the US really wants to be able to compete against China. China is not slowing down at all." (Thu, Nov 5)

$APLD CEO: Bank construction lending, project financing and bond markets remain available, although interest rates and credit spreads have risen

"The big risk is delivering on time." "The demand picture is extremely robust." (Mon, Nov 2)

$QCOM CEO: "It's not demand bound. It's a supply bound." 

"We're short on wafers, we're short on substrate, we're short on assembly. Everything is short because demand is very, very high." 

"I think what the market is reacting to is what is the speed of the compute build out."

$META on political risk: "We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of the platform.

Say as soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet because we don't want to lose this investment in our town. We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere." (Wed, Nov 4)

Even politicians campaigning against data centers are negotiating. But Meta's president also emphasized that starting new US DCs will become more difficult. 

TLDR:
-> Extremely bullish commentary from accelerator players, networking, and semi companies
-> DC developers report strong pricing/demand, but increasingly emphasize financing, permitting and execution risks (more cautious)
-> Politicians that previously campaigned against DCs are showing cooperation

tweets.full_text:
Various commentary from Qualcomm, Arm, to Meta executives this week during the AI selloff: 

$LITE CEO: "You had a comment from the CEO of $IREN and I'd second that. There's a massive disconnect in what we're seeing in our demand books. 

And what the markets are showing. And yet you're seeing a massive, massive selloff." (Fri, Nov 6)

$AMD CEO CNBC: "We're at the very beginning of the adoption cycle, where people can see where AI and superintelligence will take us" 

"We are seeing demand being higher than supply" (Wed, Nov 4)

$ARM CEO regarding a debate whether AI infrastructure spending is about to peak:

"I think in some states where it gets harder, other states may pick it up to make it easier, but I do believe strongly that if the US hesitates in any way shape performance in terms of data center buildout...

"The rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity. And I think globally the US really wants to be able to compete against China. China is not slowing down at all." (Thu, Nov 5)

$APLD CEO: Bank construction lending, project financing and bond markets remain available, although interest rates and credit spreads have risen

"The big risk is delivering on time." "The demand picture is extremely robust." (Mon, Nov 2)

$QCOM CEO: "It's not demand bound. It's a supply bound." 

"We're short on wafers, we're short on substrate, we're short on assembly. Everything is short because demand is very, very high." 

"I think what the market is reacting to is what is the speed of the compute build out."

$META on political risk: "We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of the platform.

Say as soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet because we don't want to lose this investment in our town. We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere." (Wed, Nov 4)

Even politicians campaigning against data centers are negotiating. But Meta's president also emphasized that starting new US DCs will become more difficult. 

TLDR:
-> Extremely bullish commentary from accelerator players, networking, and semi companies
-> DC developers report strong pricing/demand, but increasingly emphasize financing, permitting and execution risks (more cautious)
-> Politicians that previously campaigned against DCs are showing cooperation

There's an important difference between demand disappearing and demand being delayed by the inability to build fast enough.

Despite the severity of the selloff, I'm not seeing evidence of widespread AI demand destruction in commentary.

tweets.text:
It think it's stupid that "AI Bubble" gets used over and over. In infra names you have: 

- 1-3x fwd P/E memory companies from Samsung to $ESMT. With HBM players now having hyperscaler multi-year price floor LTAs. 

- Optical companies like $POET traded -$97M under net cash. Valuing the operating business very negatively, not even at $0. 

- While AI companies with larger premiums continue to record demand over the next 3-5 years. Such as the new $20B LTAs signed w/ $COHR to $5B LTAs signed w/ $LITE. 

Can someone in the media honestly see negative EV high-beta optical companies, where 2 years of burnrate would still value the company below $0.  

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

Many of these names are extremely profitable today... 

But obviously there's other elements inside the theme, such as: 

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously. 

But everything gets grouped into one with the boogyman of "leverage" or "debt". 

Yes, valuations can compress or correct from macro, potential regulatory uncertainty, or potential capex reductions. 

But for the companies physically powering the AI buildout, it looks more like the Great AI Deleveraging of 2026... 

Than anything like fundamental demand destruction.

As more earnings come out and free cash flow accumulates over time.

I'm confident in a recovery, especially in bottlenecks, and for markets to eventually discern durability + growth over frothy valuations tied to AI.

tweets.text:
correct, this is the stablecoin trilemma (made up term, dont think anyone ever wrote this down):

between three properties of 
1) crypto-backed/immutable
2) solvent
3) scalable,
a stablecoin can only choose 2 of 3. 

old-dai, lusd chose 1+2 (sacrifice scalability)
usdt, usdc choose 2+3 (sacrifice immutability)
terrausd and its many clones chose 1+3 (sacrifice solvency)

note that the three choices not equal: 
- a stablecoin that isnt solvent fails its single most important test.
- give that money's utility scales with its network, sacrificing scalability is a large price that ultimately dooms the coin to failure
- immutability, then, is arguably the least-bad thing to sacrifice, because ("the only free lunch") it can be at least partially addressed with diversification. you also become less vulnerable with scale (see tether being a huge holder of t-bills giving it a certain political immunity)

“No Más.” — Roberto Durán

This was the week it felt like investors finally threw in the white towel on the AI trade.

The S&P 500 was down just 2.7% for the week, but it felt far worse. The real damage wasn't in the index. It was in the hedge fund world, where what looked like a capitulation moment triggered a cascade of forced selling across hedge funds, leveraged ETFs, and CTAs. The Nasdaq 100 (NDX/QQQ) finished down 5% for the week, with more than 100% of that decline occurring in just two hours on Thursday, between 8:30 and 10:30 a.m. New York time.

The magnitude of the deleveraging was extraordinary. Volatility spiked, put-call ratios reached extremes, trading volumes exploded, and hedge funds cut exposure at a historic pace. Hedge fund closure rumors went viral.

And I was buying into the panic.  

In this week's video, I explain why I would try and catch a falling knife and why I believe we're witnessing a market structure deleveraging event rather than a breakdown in AI fundamentals or the economy. I go through the data behind the forced selling, the factor signals I'm watching for exhaustion, and why the midterm results may have actually reduced the risk of an AI bubble.

I also explore the changing market structure, the emerging importance of factor rotations, and why declining liquidity headwinds could be a significant positive for AI, Bitcoin, and gold.

The AI revolution is a long-duration investment opportunity being traded in an increasingly short-duration market.

Investing is becoming a counterpuncher's game. The market structure has changed forever and hedge fund leverage has forever peaked.

Watch the full weekly update:
https://t.co/81rUCu9FkG

tweets.text:
Apple finally stepping up to compete in AI with a personal AI agent that rivals Meta Muse, grok bot etc. few thoughts:

- the new feature would allow 3rd-party apps to integrate siri. which means siri can perform actions, pull context through every app on your phone. that’s pretty sick.

- despite being behind in AI, apple has a huge advantage: 3.5 billion devices people love and use everyday 

- but at the same time siri right now sucks, is incapable of doing even 30% of the things frontier LLMs can do. it can’t even use a computer.

- compare this to muse, dots or grok bot that can work autonomously 24/7, self-improving the more you use it AND have access to their own computer. they’re miles ahead.

imo apple has to balance delivering quickly (& aggressively) on AI without causing a major security breach. their whole thing is trust and privacy.

that’s the challenge ternus will face.

thread_tweets.text: Imagine you are put in charge of monitoring a massive water tank the size of a football stadium. The water inside doubles in volume every sixty seconds. At 12:00 noon, the tank overflows. When should you have become concerned? At 11:59 the tank was only half full.
thread_tweets.quoted_tweet_text: The reason humans have such difficulty judging exponential growth is how rarely examples of it appeared in the ancestral environment. As a result, it was absent from our training data. For us, exponential growth is an out-of-distribution problem.
